title: Electric Potential

title: Current and Resistance
blurb: A metal wire contains an enormous number of free electrons. When a battery is connected, an electric field is set up inside the wire and pushes on all of them. They collide with the atomic lattice constantly, so their average drift velocity is small (around a millimeter per second), but the whole population starts drifting at the same time, which is why a circuit responds almost instantly.

title: DC Circuits and Kirchhoff's Rules
blurb: A pump analogy captures most of how circuits behave: A battery acts like a pump: it raises each coulomb of charge to a higher potential. The rise per coulomb is the emf . A resistor is where that potential is used up: charge drops in potential as it passes through. An ideal wire has no resistance, so there is no potential change along it. Going all the way around any closed loop returns you to the same potential you started from.

title: RC Circuits
blurb: When an uncharged capacitor is connected to a battery through a resistor, the current is largest at the start, because an empty capacitor has no voltage opposing the battery. As charge builds up, the capacitor's voltage opposes the battery more and more, so the current falls off exponentially. The capacitor approaches full charge asymptotically; after a few time constants it is effectively full.

title: Magnetic Fields from Currents: Biot–Savart
blurb: A current in a long straight wire produces magnetic field lines that form circles centered on the wire.

title: Magnetic Forces and the Hall Effect
blurb: The magnetic force on a charge has three distinctive properties: It is zero for a charge at rest. It is zero for a charge moving parallel to the field. It is always perpendicular to both the velocity and the field, so it changes the direction of motion but never the speed. A magnetic force does no work.

title: Magnetic Materials and Field Energy
blurb: Every atom has tiny current loops (electrons orbiting and spinning), so every atom can act like a tiny magnet.
